analysis.one_liner: Freezes new Safe Drinking Water Act rules until EPA completes studies and Congress reauthorizes the law.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the EPA from implementing any national drinking water regulation issued after December 21, 1989 — a window that includes rules adopted in the early 1990s — until the EPA finished a sweeping review of existing rules, compliance deadlines, and funding needs, and until Congress enacted a law reauthorizing the Safe Drinking Water Act. It included an escape valve: the EPA could still act on a rule if it found immediate implementation was needed to protect human health.
analysis.who_benefits: Public water systems — especially small ones — that would have avoided or delayed the cost of complying with drinking water standards, and any industries whose contaminants the delayed rules would have addressed.

how_it_helps.text: Blocks implementation of any national primary drinking water regulation promulgated after December 21, 1989 until the EPA meets the bill's study requirements and Congress enacts reauthorization legislation [S3].

Requires the EPA to study each final regulation, regulatory alternatives at different safety levels and their system-level costs, the contaminant list, compliance deadlines, whether some rules should apply only to small systems, and state funding needs [S3].
Lets the EPA skip the moratorium and implement a rule immediately if it determines, in consultation with the states, that it is justifiable to protect human health [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who drink from public water systems, who would wait longer for enforceable limits on contaminants while the studies and a reauthorization bill moved through Congress.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium would delay enforcement of drinking water standards for up to a year of study, plus however long Congress took to reauthorize the Act — and if reauthorization stalled, the freeze would have no end date [S3].
The moratorium covers all regulations issued after December 21, 1989, not just burdensome ones, so health-protective standards already on the books would not be implemented while the review ran [S3].
The bill's exemption only applies when the EPA itself affirmatively finds immediate implementation justified, shifting the burden onto the regulator rather than the regulated systems [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument on the cost side: drinking water rules can impose significant compliance expenses, and small water systems feel those most, which is why the bill asked for a cost and funding study. But the bill's remedy was to freeze all recent rules — including health-protective ones — until both a lengthy review and a full reauthorization of the Act were complete, with no deadline on the reauthorization. The delay falls on the people who drink the water, and the pause could be indefinite.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health and the Environment subcommittee, neither of which ever acted on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Skeen introduced the bill on August 4, 1992, with 13 cosponsors (10 Republicans, 3 Democrats) [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day [S5].
On September 14, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where it remained with no further action [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993, and the bill received no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the drinking water regulations issued since late 1989 stayed enforceable, and water systems did not get the compliance delay it would have created. The beneficiaries of the outcome are the people who drink from public water systems; the moratorium's intended beneficiaries never got it.

for.name: Rep. Joe Skeen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought a moratorium on new drinking water regulations pending studies and reauthorization of the Safe Drinking Water Act.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral on August 4, 1992.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and the Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 14, 1992 and held no markup or further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was Republican and 10 of 13 cosponsors were Republicans, but 3 Democrats signed on and there were no votes to reveal a partisan split.

industries.note: The moratorium would have suspended implementation of drinking water regulations promulgated after December 21, 1989, delaying compliance costs for water systems — including a specific review of whether some rules should apply only to small systems [S3]. The cost of that delay would fall on the people the rules protect, so the systems' interest in this bill ran against the public's. The bill died, so the rules stayed in force.

industries.industry: Small water utilities and small communities
industries.note: The bill directed the EPA to study whether regulations should apply exclusively to small public water systems and to assess state and local funding needs [S3]. It never passed, so no relief was delivered.
